items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the DSM-5 classification of schizophrenia. Include at least one point about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): A diagnosis allows access to treatment and research on causes and treatments. Strength (reliability): Clear criteria with listed symptoms and time periods help different clinicians reach the same diagnosis. Weakness (ethics): A label of schizophrenia can lead to stigma and discrimination in work and relationships. Weakness (validity): Two people diagnosed with schizophrenia can share no symptoms at all, which suggests the category may combine different disorders. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Explain the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia.
items.answer: It proposes that excess dopamine activity (too much dopamine or too many/oversensitive D2 receptors), especially in the mesolimbic pathway, causes positive symptoms such as hallucinations; low dopamine activity in the prefrontal cortex may relate to negative symptoms.

items.stem: “The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including supporting evidence in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It led to the development of antipsychotic drugs that allow many patients to live in the community. Strength (supporting evidence): Antipsychotic drugs that block D2 receptors reduce positive symptoms, and amphetamines that raise dopamine can cause psychosis, supporting a role for dopamine. Weakness (negative symptoms): It explains positive symptoms better than negative symptoms, which respond poorly to dopamine-blocking drugs. Weakness (reductionism): It reduces a complex disorder to one neurotransmitter, ignoring glutamate, genes, cognition and social factors. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Evaluate drug therapy (antipsychotics) for schizophrenia, including a discussion of effectiveness.
items.answer: Strength (cost and practicality): Drugs are relatively cheap and need little therapist time compared with psychological therapies. Strength (effectiveness): Antipsychotics reduce positive symptoms for many patients within weeks, allowing them to leave hospital and live in the community. Weakness (side effects): Typical antipsychotics can cause tardive dyskinesia and atypicals can cause weight gain, so many patients stop taking them. Weakness (ethics): Drugs may be used to control patients rather than to help them, and some are given medication without full informed consent. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss whether drug treatments are the most effective way of managing schizophrenia.
items.answer: Arguments for: Antipsychotics reduce positive symptoms quickly for many patients and allow them to live in the community. They are relatively cheap and easy to administer. Arguments against: Side effects (tardive dyskinesia with typical drugs; weight gain and agranulocytosis risk with clozapine) reduce adherence. They treat symptoms, not causes, and are less effective for negative symptoms. CBT (Sensky et al., 2000) and token economies (Paul and Lentz, 1977) improve functioning. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.answer: The therapist helps the patient to examine the evidence for delusions, to see voices as a product of their own mind, and to develop coping strategies, reducing distress and improving functioning.

items.stem: Elena, a man with schizophrenia in Lisbon, has taken chlorpromazine for five years. His hallucinations are reduced, but he has developed involuntary lip-smacking and rarely leaves his room. Suggest a different drug treatment and explain one advantage of it.
items.answer: An atypical antipsychotic such as clozapine, which causes fewer movement side effects and may help negative symptoms.

items.answer: Correct. It is a perception without an external stimulus.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength of the DSM-5 classification of schizophrenia in terms of reliability.
items.answer: Clear criteria with listed symptoms and time periods help different clinicians reach the same diagnosis.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to reliability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Mohammed compared symptom severity (0–50) for patients given medication with CBT or medication alone in Cairo. Table: Symptom score (0–50) — Medication plus CBT: 25, 13, 22, 16, 30, 22, 18, 23. Medication only: 18, 21, 29, 27, 28, 25, 26, 27. Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here.
items.answer: Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that drug treatments are the most effective way of managing schizophrenia.
items.answer: Arguments for: Antipsychotics reduce positive symptoms quickly for many patients and allow them to live in the community. They are relatively cheap and easy to administer. Arguments against: Side effects (tardive dyskinesia with typical drugs; weight gain and agranulocytosis risk with clozapine) reduce adherence. They treat symptoms, not causes, and are less effective for negative symptoms. CBT (Sensky et al., 2000) and token economies (Paul and Lentz, 1977) improve functioning. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Daniel, aged 22, from Lagos, has stopped going to university. For the past seven months Daniel has believed that neighbours are reading their thoughts, hears a voice commenting on everything they do, and rarely speaks or washes. (a) Identify one positive and one negative symptom shown by Daniel. (b) Explain whether Daniel meets the DSM-5 time criterion for schizophrenia. (c) Explain one reason why a clinician should be careful before diagnosing Daniel.
items.answer: (a) Positive: delusion that neighbours read their thoughts, or auditory hallucination (a commenting voice). Negative: alogia (rarely speaks) or avolition (not washing, not attending university). (b) Yes: symptoms have lasted seven months, more than the six months of continuous signs required, with active symptoms for more than one month. (c) The symptoms could be caused by drug use, a medical condition or a mood disorder with psychotic features, which must be ruled out; cultural beliefs must also be considered.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark yes; 1 mark six-month criterion [2] (c) 1 mark alternative cause; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The ability to reflect on one’s own thoughts and intentions and recognise them as one’s own”?
items.answer: Metarepresentation
items.markingKey: Metarepresentation: the ability to reflect on one’s own thoughts and intentions and recognise them as one’s own. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “The diathesis–stress model combines biological vulnerability with environmental triggers.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia.
items.answer: (a) Correct. It explains why not everyone with a genetic risk develops the disorder. (b) It proposes that excess dopamine activity (too much dopamine or too many/oversensitive D2 receptors), especially in the mesolimbic pathway, causes positive symptoms such as hallucinations; low dopamine activity in the prefrontal cortex may relate to negative symptoms.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark excess dopamine/receptors; 1 mark link to positive symptoms; 1 mark pathway or negative symptoms [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia. (b) Explain how twin studies are used to investigate genetic factors in schizophrenia.
items.answer: (a) It proposes that excess dopamine activity (too much dopamine or too many/oversensitive D2 receptors), especially in the mesolimbic pathway, causes positive symptoms such as hallucinations; low dopamine activity in the prefrontal cortex may relate to negative symptoms. (b) Concordance rates for identical (MZ) twins, who share 100% of their genes, are compared with fraternal (DZ) twins, who share about 50%; higher MZ concordance suggests a genetic contribution.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark excess dopamine/receptors; 1 mark link to positive symptoms; 1 mark pathway or negative symptoms [3] (b) 1 mark MZ v DZ; 1 mark interpretation [2]

items.stem: Mateo analysed national records of children in Lima according to whether their parents had schizophrenia. Children with both parents with schizophrenia: 273 followed up, 61 diagnosed with schizophrenia. Children with one parent with schizophrenia: 1080 followed up, 77 diagnosed with schizophrenia. Children with neither parent with schizophrenia: 26274 followed up, 209 diagnosed with schizophrenia. Calculate the percentage of children with neither parent with schizophrenia who were diagnosed with schizophrenia. Give your answer to one decimal place.
items.markingKey: 209 ÷ 26274 × 100 = 0.8%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Twins Diego and Felix grew up in Bangkok. Diego was diagnosed with schizophrenia at 23 after a stressful year; Felix has not developed it. (a) Explain what this case suggests if the twins are identical (MZ). (b) Use the diathesis–stress model to explain why Diego developed schizophrenia.
items.answer: (a) They share all their genes, so the difference shows that genes alone do not cause schizophrenia; environmental factors such as stress matter. (b) Diego may have inherited a vulnerability (diathesis), and the stressful year acted as a trigger that led to onset.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark same genes; 1 mark environment needed [2] (b) 1 mark diathesis; 1 mark stress trigger [2]

items.stem: Design a questionnaire to investigate how family members feel about caring for a relative with schizophrenia. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, the types of questions and ethical issues.
items.answer: Method: a questionnaire. Closed questions (for example rating scales from 1 to 5) for quantitative data and at least one open question for qualitative detail; pilot the questions; avoid leading questions. Variables: topic: experiences of carers; measure: rating scales and open answers. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Dubai, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘tardive dyskinesia’?
items.answer: Involuntary movements of the face and body that can develop after long-term use of typical antipsychotics.
items.markingKey: Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary movements of the face and body that can develop after long-term use of typical antipsychotics. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how typical antipsychotic drugs reduce the symptoms of schizophrenia. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “CBT is often used alongside medication rather than instead of it.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) They block dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway, reducing excessive dopamine transmission and so reducing positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions. (b) Correct. CBT helps patients cope with symptoms that remain while they take medication.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark block D2; 1 mark reduce positive symptoms [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how a token economy could be used with patients with schizophrenia. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “CBT is often used alongside medication rather than instead of it.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Target behaviours such as self-care or attending activities are defined; patients receive tokens immediately after performing them; tokens are exchanged for rewards such as snacks or outings, reinforcing the behaviours (operant conditioning). (b) Correct. CBT helps patients cope with symptoms that remain while they take medication.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark target behaviours; 1 mark tokens; 1 mark exchange/reinforcement [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: ‘Schizophrenia is best explained by biological factors.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology. In your answer, you may refer to nature versus nurture, the diathesis–stress model and reductionism.
items.answer: Arguments for: Twin and family studies show a genetic component: Gottesman et al. (2010) found about 27% of children with two parents with schizophrenia developed it, compared with under 1% of children of unaffected parents. The dopamine hypothesis is supported by the effects of amphetamines and of antipsychotics that block D2 receptors. Arguments against: Concordance in identical twins is well below 100%, so environment must matter. Cognitive explanations (Frith’s faulty self-monitoring) explain hallucinations as misattributed inner speech. Stress and family environment can trigger onset (diathesis–stress). Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
